# OpenSSH Hardening & Post-Quantum Key Exchange

::: {.callout-note}
**Part 08: Security, Cryptography & Hardening** · Section 8.3  
*Ubuntu 26.04 LTS ("Resolute Raccoon") Reference Platform*
:::

## Executive Summary & Objectives

This chapter establishes the engineering foundations, operational mental models, and production workflows for **OpenSSH Hardening & Post-Quantum Key Exchange** within modern Ubuntu 26.04 LTS environments.

## Syllabus & Focus Areas

- [ ] **OpenSSH 10.2 hardening on Ubuntu 26.04 (check updates and client compatibility):** `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf`, Post-Quantum Key Exchange (`mlkem768x25519-sha256`), Ed25519 & FIDO2 hardware keys (`ed25519-sk`), disabling password & root auth, `sshd.service` alias
- [ ] **Brute-Force & Connection Defense:** OpenSSH native `PerSourcePenalties` (crash/auth failure throttling), `MaxStartups`, `LoginGraceTime`, `AllowUsers`/`AllowGroups`, `Match` blocks
- [ ] **SSH Certificate Authority (CA):** Eliminating TOFU & `authorized_keys` sprawl: `ssh-keygen` CA creation, signing user & host keys with principals and TTLs, `TrustedUserCAKeys`, `RevokedKeys` (KRL)
- [ ] **Bastions, Tunnels & Multiplexing:** `ProxyJump` (`-J`), local (`-L`), remote (`-R`), and dynamic SOCKS (`-D`) port forwarding, Unix domain socket forwarding, `ControlMaster` multiplexing, `sftp` chroot jails

## Architectural Concepts & Mental Model

Understanding the subsystem architecture, system boundary layers, and kernel-userspace interactions:

- **Target Release Context:** Standardized on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS defaults (Linux 7.0 generic kernel, pure `cgroup v2`, `sudo-rs`, OpenSSH 10.2).
- **Core Abstractions:** Subsystem primitives, state machines, and configuration hierarchies.
- **Integration Points:** Interaction with `systemd`, security layers (AppArmor 4.x), and network/storage fabrics.

## Common Traps, Failure Modes & Recovery

| Symptom / Failure Mode | Root Cause | Safe Remediation & Recovery |
|------------------------|------------|-----------------------------|
| Service startup failure / degraded state | Configuration syntax or permission mismatch | Inspect unit status and journal logs (`journalctl -xeu <unit>`) |
| Unintended state mutation | Legacy utility flag discrepancies | Verify command semantics against `rust-coreutils` and `sudo-rs` |
| Latency or resource starvation | Unbounded resource exhaustion | Check cgroup pressure metrics (`/proc/pressure/*`) |
